extracted.intended_audience: aspiring sitcom writers and comedy creators (e.g., competition entrants, pilot writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, experience-based guidance for writing half-hour TV sitcom scripts and pilots, covering structure, characters, plotting, and script polish. Aimed at writers preparing scripts for competitions, submissions, or production in a studio/stage-style sitcom format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sitcom formula: Character + Conflict + Confinement = Comedy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author takes this formula as a foundational assumption for sitcoms — the combination of distinct characters, clear conflict, and a constrained setting produces comedy. This is treated as a starting lens for the following rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1: Your characters and situation don't change
rubrics_metrics.description: A sitcom is, to some extent, the same show every week: the same characters make the same mistakes and don't change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should largely remain static across episodes: they may talk about big changes (e.g., moving to another country) but they do not actually change or learn permanently. Episodes can show a 'lesson' but the characters should revert by the next week. This constancy helps preserve the comedic premise and repeatable dynamics; exceptions can be powerful but are not sustainable as weekly practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 2: You've got 48 hours!
rubrics_metrics.description: Sitcoms normally take place in a 24 to 48 hour time span; three days often feels too long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the episode's timeframe tight (about 1–2 days) so events (parties, meetings) remain plausible and momentum is preserved. Exceptions include deliberate real-time episodes (examples: Miranda at the psychiatrist; Seinfeld episode waiting for a table). The implicit time compression is accepted by audiences familiar with TV conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 3: Start your story ASAP
rubrics_metrics.description: Given limited time and page count, start the story as soon as possible and give main characters achievable goals early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With only ~32 pages to tell the story (studio half-hour format), avoid long stretches of talk without action; many scripts waste pages before launching the main plot. Introduce clear, achievable goals early so characters' choices and comedic complications can develop within the short timeframe. Show character via action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 4: Give your characters HELL
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your characters' lives an utter misery and make their goals suddenly seem far away or impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After setting achievable goals, escalate obstacles so the characters struggle — but don't simply contrive suffering. Provide believable reasons for characters to make bad choices or head into disaster (conflicting goals, misunderstandings). Ask why this day is the worst possible day for that goal. Use conflict and complication to generate comedy. (Author links to further blog posts on the subject and an example by Chuck Wendig.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 5: Keep it simple
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep storylines simple: confusion is the enemy of comedy; if the audience doesn't know what's happening they won't laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly complicated plots or many interlocking elements that make the audience struggle to follow. Prioritize clear plotting and broad comedic beats. For examples of clear plotting, watch shows like The Goldbergs. Simplicity helps jokes land and audiences stay engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 6: Don't get caught by the logic police
rubrics_metrics.description: Every action taken by your characters must have a believable reason and make sense to them, not be a convenient contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain internal logic: actions should follow character motivation and plausible incentives. If audience members are asking 'No-one would ever do that,' the episode's reality is undermined. Make sure choices feel earned. (The author notes there are caveats — some rule-bending is allowed at climactic moments per Rule 7.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 7: Go big at the end
rubrics_metrics.description: At the very end of the script you can push things further and get away with things that slightly overstep logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the final moments as a topper: sequences that would be borderline earlier can work as a surprising or visually funny payoff (example: main character returns to find living room full of mini-wind-up robots mentioned earlier). The last two minutes let you stretch plausibility for comedic payoff, but it should feel like a topper rather than a character doing something totally out of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8: No coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: A chance event cannot solve your character's big problem; resolution must come from actions by characters, ideally at cost to themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid late-breaking information or deus ex machina. The solution should arise from character agency or something set up earlier in the episode (often a regular character finally doing something obvious). Don't introduce new information in the last third. Resolutions should feel earned and logically connected to the plot and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 9: Avoid outside characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit use of outside/guest characters — audiences want the regulars; outside characters should only exist to make regulars do funny things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer using established regular characters to generate comedy (e.g., have a known regular volunteer as a trainer instead of introducing a one-off personal trainer). Outside characters can be exciting but risk distracting from the ensemble; they should primarily serve to reveal or push the regulars. Building a large recurring family of characters can wait until later series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10: Avoid outside locations
rubrics_metrics.description: For studio sitcoms, minimize outside locations and stage most action (especially the denouement) in front of the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat filming like a play rather than a movie: keep scenes on primary sets to preserve performance energy and audience engagement. Limit location shoots which fragment the theatrical feel and make it harder to stage comedic payoffs for a live audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 11: Make those first lines count
rubrics_metrics.description: In a pilot, ensure the first line spoken by each main character is significant and reveals something important about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First impressions matter: give each main character a strong first line, a prop, or a distinctive piece of clothing to reinforce who they are. How we first encounter characters creates a lasting impression, so use openings to establish voice and defining traits that pay off later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 12: Be brutal
rubrics_metrics.description: Be ruthless in editing: every line should be a joke, a character line, or a plot development (ideally at least two of those).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After writing, put the script aside and then revise with a pen, cutting any line that isn't serving joke, character, or plot. Tight scripts beat baggy ones: aim for a tight ~29-page script rather than a sprawling 40-pager. The author emphasizes ruthless pruning and links to more on polishing scripts and personal lessons learned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 13: Do what you want
rubrics_metrics.description: You can write about anything; write in your original voice about things you're passionate about rather than following perceived commissioner trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you're not a writer-performer you have freedom to write about any characters/ages/locations — your own acting persona is not limiting. Don't be swayed solely by stories of what commissioners want; ultimately commissioners seek something funny. Original voice and passion are likelier to produce genuinely funny material than cynical or hacky imitation.
